definition: A user-defined type that bundles data members and the functions that operate on them.
wrongs: One instance that already contains the values of a particular object.
A namespace, which cannot give its members private access.
A single variable of a built-in type.
why: The class describes layout and behaviour, while objects created from it hold the actual member values.
example: A Counter type declares a count and an increment operation, but that declaration is not itself a counter value.
scenario: A programmer specifies the data and operations of a Counter, and no counter storage exists until an instance is created. What was specified?
scenarioWhy: The declaration describes the type, and later instances are objects of that class.

definition: A region of storage of some type; for a class type, one instance holding that class's member values.
wrongs: The source text that defines a class and contains no per-instance values.
A header file that only declares a class.
A function template before any instantiation.
why: Creating an instance allocates its members and runs a constructor so there is a usable value.
example: The declaration Counter c creates one Counter instance named c.
scenario: The statement Counter c allocates storage and runs a constructor. What does the name c denote?
scenarioWhy: c names an instance with its own storage, which is an object of the class.

definition: Bundling data with the operations on that data while restricting outside access to the representation.
wrongs: Giving one function name several parameter lists chosen at compile time.
Deriving a new class from an existing class.
Allocating an instance with new.
why: Callers use the public operations, so the private layout can change without changing those callers.
example: A stack type offers push and pop, and client code cannot reach the private array that stores the items.
scenario: Clients of a stack may call push and pop, but they cannot read the private array inside the stack. Which idea is that?
scenarioWhy: The data and operations are bundled, and the representation is hidden from clients.

definition: A label such as public, protected, or private that sets which code may use the members that follow.
wrongs: A keyword that chooses whether an object is created on the stack or the heap.
A keyword that changes the width of int.
A label that marks a function as recursive.
why: Members keep the accessibility of the latest specifier until another specifier appears.
example: Members written after private can be used by the class's own functions but not by main.
scenario: A data member can be used by the class's member functions and not by main. Which specifier states that restriction?
scenarioWhy: private members are available to the class and its friends, not to unrelated functions such as main.

definition: A special member function, with no return type, that initializes an object when the object is created.
wrongs: A member function that runs when an object's lifetime ends.
An ordinary function that returns a new value and is not tied to creation.
A function used only to copy an existing object and never for any other creation.
why: Creation must establish a valid initial state, and this function is the place that does so.
example: Creating a Counter runs a function that sets its count member to 0 before any other call.
scenario: Creating a Counter sets its count to 0 before any normal member function runs. Which function did that initialization?
scenarioWrongs: A free function that returns a Counter
scenarioWhy: Initialization performed as part of creating the object is the constructor's job.

definition: A constructor that can be called with no arguments.
wrongs: A constructor that requires one or more arguments.
The constructor used to initialize an object from another object of the same type.
A destructor, because a destructor also has an empty parameter list.
why: A declaration that supplies no constructor arguments needs a constructor that can be invoked with none.
example: The declaration Sensor s with no parentheses calls a constructor that takes no arguments.
scenario: The declaration Sensor s must compile and initialize s without any arguments. Which constructor is required?
scenarioWrongs: A constructor that requires an int
scenarioWhy: No arguments are provided, so the class needs a constructor that can be called with an empty argument list.

definition: A constructor that accepts arguments and uses them to initialize the new object.
wrongs: A constructor that can be called with no arguments.
An assignment that changes an object which already exists.
A destructor that receives the object's final values.
why: The arguments provide the initial state at the moment the object is created.
example: Creating a point with the arguments 3 and 4 initializes its coordinates from those arguments.
scenario: The declaration of point p passes 3 and 4, and p is created with those coordinates. Which constructor runs?
scenarioWhy: The coordinates are arguments used to initialize a newly created object.

definition: A constructor that initializes a new object as a copy of another object of the same type.
wrongs: An assignment operator that copies into an object which already exists.
A constructor that takes no arguments.
A destructor that copies resources out before releasing them.
why: Copy initialization creates a new object, including when an argument is passed by value.
example: Passing a string by value copy-constructs the parameter from the caller's string.
scenario: String b is created from an existing string a. Which special member initializes b?
scenarioWhy: b is a new object initialized from a, so this is copy construction rather than assignment.

definition: The member function that runs when an object's lifetime ends and releases resources the object owns.
wrongs: The function that initializes an object when its lifetime begins.
The function that initializes a new object from an existing one.
A function the programmer must call by name to end every automatic object.
why: Automatic objects are destroyed when their scope ends, and this function is the cleanup hook.
example: When a local file object leaves its block, its destructor closes the handle the constructor opened.
scenario: A local file object leaves its block, and the handle it owns is closed automatically. Which function closed the handle?
scenarioWrongs: A manual free that automatic objects always require
scenarioWhy: Leaving the scope ends the object's lifetime and therefore runs the destructor.

definition: The part of a constructor, before the body, that initializes bases and members.
wrongs: Assignments inside the constructor body, which can initialize a const member.
The parameter list of an ordinary member function.
The list of automatic objects destroyed when a scope ends.
why: Members and bases are initialized before the constructor body executes, which is required for const members and references.
example: A constructor sets a const id from a parameter in the initializer list because a const member cannot be assigned in the body.
scenario: A class has a const int id that must receive its value when the object is created. Where must that initialization be written?
scenarioWrongs: In an assignment in the constructor body
Only in a setter called later
scenarioWhy: A const member is initialized before the constructor body and cannot be assigned later.

definition: The pointer inside a non-static member function that addresses the object on which the function was called.
wrongs: A pointer to the single copy of a static data member.
A hidden argument passed to a static member function.
A pointer that addresses only a different object from the one used in the call.
why: The call is made on a particular object, and this names that object inside the function.
example: Inside Counter increment, this reaches the count of the Counter on which increment was called.
scenario: increment is called on object c and must name c's own count. Which pointer inside the function addresses c?
scenarioWrongs: A pointer to the class type
scenarioWhy: A non-static member function receives the address of the object used in the call as this.

definition: A member function that promises not to modify the object and that may be called on a const object.
wrongs: A function whose return type is const but that may still change the object.
A static member function, which can carry a const qualifier.
A constructor, which is always a const member function.
why: The const qualifier after the parameter list makes this a pointer to const, so ordinary members cannot be assigned.
example: A size function declared const can be called on a const list and cannot push a new element.
scenario: A const rectangle must support a call to area, and that call must compile. How should area be declared?
scenarioWrongs: As a static function marked const
scenarioWhy: Only a const member function may be called on a const object.

definition: A class member of which there is one copy shared by all objects, rather than one copy in each object.
wrongs: A member stored separately inside every object.
A local static variable inside a free function.
A member that each constructor must initialize separately for its own object.
why: The member belongs to the class, so a change made through one object is visible through every other object.
example: A live-object counter in Counter is increased by every constructor, and every Counter sees that same counter.
scenario: Every Counter must see one shared tally of live objects, not a separate tally inside each counter. Where should the tally be declared?
scenarioWrongs: As an ordinary member of each object
scenarioWhy: A static data member is the single class-wide object shared by all instances.

definition: A mechanism by which a derived class receives the members of a base class and may add or override behaviour.
wrongs: Storing an object of another type as a member, without deriving from that type.
Hiding data behind private access without any derived class.
Declaring several functions that share a name but have different parameters.
why: A derived object contains a base subobject, so it can reuse the base members.
example: A Dog declared to derive from Animal can use Animal's eat operation and add its own bark operation.
scenario: Dog is declared to derive from Animal and receives Animal's members. Which mechanism is that?
scenarioWhy: Deriving Dog from Animal makes Dog reuse Animal through inheritance.

definition: The class from which another class inherits members.
wrongs: The class that is declared to inherit from another class.
A free function used by a class.
The most derived complete object created by a variable definition.
why: The base declares the common members that each derived class receives as a subobject.
example: In a declaration of Dog that derives from Animal, Animal is the class being inherited from.
scenario: Dog derives from Animal. Which of those classes is the base?
scenarioWhy: The class named as the one being inherited from is the base class.

definition: A class that inherits from a base class and may add members or override virtual functions.
wrongs: The class named as the source of inherited members.
A base object produced by copying away the extra derived members.
A namespace nested inside a class.
why: The derived class extends the base and contains the base as a subobject.
example: Dog inherits from Animal and adds bark, so Dog is the class that extends Animal.
scenario: Animal is inherited from, and Dog adds bark. Which class is derived?
scenarioWrongs: An Animal copy of a Dog
scenarioWhy: Dog is the class that inherits, so Dog is the derived class.

definition: Access that lets a class and classes derived from it use a member, while unrelated code cannot.
wrongs: Access that lets any function in the program use the member.
Access that lets only the declaring class and its friends use the member, not derived classes.
Access that limits a member to a single function body.
why: It is broader than private, so descendants can use details that ordinary clients still cannot use.
example: A protected hunger member of Animal can be changed by a Dog method and cannot be changed by main.
scenario: A Dog method reads hunger, main cannot read hunger, and hunger is not public. Which access allows the Dog method?
scenarioWhy: protected members are available to derived classes and hidden from unrelated functions.

definition: Supplying, in a derived class, a new definition of a virtual base function with the same signature.
wrongs: Declaring another function of the same name with a different parameter list in one class.
Hiding a non-virtual base function so a base pointer still calls the base version.
Generating a function from a template for a new type.
why: Because the base function is virtual, a call through a base pointer or reference uses the derived definition.
example: Dog replaces Animal's virtual speak, and an Animal pointer to a Dog runs Dog's speak.
scenario: Dog defines virtual speak with the same parameters as Animal's virtual speak. What is Dog's function relative to Animal's?
scenarioWrongs: A non-virtual function with static binding
scenarioWhy: A matching definition of a virtual base function in the derived class is an override.

definition: A member function whose override is chosen at run time when the call uses a base pointer or reference.
wrongs: A function that is always bound using only the static type of the pointer.
A function template, which is instantiated at compile time.
A static member function, which may be declared virtual.
why: The call uses the dynamic type of the object, so the derived override runs.
example: Calling virtual speak through an Animal pointer that actually addresses a Dog runs Dog's speak.
scenario: An Animal pointer addresses a Dog, and the call to speak runs Dog's version. What property of speak causes that?
scenarioWrongs: It is bound only to the Animal declaration
scenarioWhy: A virtual call selects the override that belongs to the object's dynamic type.

definition: A virtual function declared equal to zero, which a concrete derived class must override.
wrongs: A virtual function that already has a final body and need not be overridden.
A non-virtual function whose result is assigned zero.
A function that has been suppressed with the delete specifier.
why: The pure specifier means this class does not provide the final implementation that a concrete class needs.
example: Shape declares area as a pure virtual function, and Circle provides the overriding area.
scenario: Shape declares virtual area as equal to zero, and a concrete Circle must implement area. What kind of function is Shape's area?
scenarioWhy: The equal-to-zero specifier makes the virtual function pure and requires a concrete derived class to override it.

definition: A class with at least one pure virtual function, which therefore cannot be instantiated.
wrongs: Any base class, including one that has no pure virtual functions.
A class that can be instantiated whenever it has a virtual destructor.
A class template that has not yet been instantiated.
why: The missing final implementation of a pure virtual function makes creating an object of that class ill-formed.
example: Shape has a pure virtual area, so a variable of type Shape is ill-formed, while a Circle variable is allowed.
scenario: Shape has one pure virtual function, and the program declares a Shape variable. What is the result?
scenarioWhy: A class that still has a pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated.

definition: Choosing, when the call executes, which virtual override to run from the object's dynamic type.
wrongs: Choosing an overloaded function at compile time from the argument types.
Generating a function from a template for one particular type.
Hiding a private member from client code.
why: One call site can run different overrides when the pointer addresses different derived objects.
example: A loop of Animal pointers calls speak, and each element runs the Dog or Cat version that matches its object.
scenario: One call through an Animal pointer runs either Dog's speak or Cat's speak, depending on the object addressed. What is that choice called?
scenarioWhy: The override is selected from the dynamic type when the virtual call executes.

definition: The per-class table of addresses of virtual functions used to dispatch a virtual call.
wrongs: A table of the private data values stored in each object.
The page table that translates virtual memory addresses.
A structure used only to call non-virtual functions.
why: A polymorphic object typically contains a hidden pointer to the table for its dynamic type.
example: A Dog object refers to Dog's table, and the speak entry in that table addresses Dog's speak.
scenario: A virtual call loads a function address from a hidden table chosen by the object's dynamic type. What is that table?
scenarioWhy: Virtual dispatch uses the dynamic type's table of function addresses.

definition: A destructor declared virtual so deleting a derived object through a base pointer destroys the complete object.
wrongs: A non-virtual destructor, which makes that delete defined and safe.
A constructor declared virtual, which the language allows.
A destructor that is virtual in every class whether or not it is declared so.
why: If the base destructor is not virtual, deleting a derived object through a base pointer has undefined behaviour.
example: Deleting an Animal pointer that addresses a Dog runs Dog's destructor because Animal's destructor is virtual.
scenario: An Animal pointer addresses a Dog created with new, and delete must run Dog's destructor. What must Animal's destructor be?
scenarioWhy: A virtual destructor in the base makes delete through a base pointer destroy the complete derived object.

definition: A blueprint from which the compiler generates a function for each set of template arguments that is used.
wrongs: One function whose parameter type is selected at run time by a virtual call.
A macro that pastes text and does not type-check the substitution.
A class that cannot be instantiated.
why: Template parameters stand for types or values, and each instantiation is a separate concrete function.
example: A max blueprint on type T yields one function for int arguments and another for double arguments.
scenario: One max blueprint is called on ints and on doubles, and the compiler produces a function for each. What is that blueprint?
scenarioWhy: The compiler instantiates a concrete function from the template for each argument type that is used.

definition: A blueprint from which the compiler generates a distinct class for each set of template arguments that is used.
wrongs: One class whose member types change while the program is running.
A blueprint that generates functions rather than types.
A namespace that contains several ordinary classes.
why: Different template arguments produce different types, such as a box of int versus a box of string.
example: The standard vector blueprint generates one class for int elements and a different class for string elements.
scenario: Box is written once, and Box of int is a different type from Box of string. What is Box?
scenarioWhy: A class template generates a separate class for each template argument list.

definition: The practice of binding a resource to an object that acquires it in the constructor and releases it in the destructor.
wrongs: Allocating every resource with a bare new and releasing it only at the end of main.
Relying on a garbage collector so destructors need not release resources.
Making every data member public.
why: If an exception unwinds the stack, automatic objects are still destroyed, so their destructors release the resources.
example: A lock guard locks a mutex in its constructor and unlocks that mutex in its destructor when the block ends.
scenario: A function throws, a local lock object is destroyed during unwinding, and the mutex is unlocked. Which practice made that reliable?
scenarioWrongs: A bare new with no matching delete
scenarioWhy: The lock object's destructor runs as the stack unwinds and releases the mutex it acquired.

definition: A smart pointer with sole ownership of an object, deleting that object when the smart pointer is destroyed.
wrongs: A smart pointer that shares ownership through a reference count.
A raw pointer that never deletes its target.
A pointer that can be copied so two owners both delete the same object.
why: Ownership is moved rather than copied, so exactly one owner deletes the object.
example: A factory returns sole ownership of a File, and the caller's smart pointer deletes that File at the end of the scope.
scenario: A factory hands off sole ownership of a File, the caller stores it in a smart pointer, and the File is deleted when that pointer ends. Which type is it?
scenarioWhy: Exclusive ownership that deletes the object with the owner is unique_ptr.

definition: A smart pointer that shares ownership with a reference count and deletes the object when the last owner is destroyed.
wrongs: A move-only smart pointer that cannot share ownership.
A non-owning observer that never changes a reference count.
A raw pointer that deletes the object every time it is copied.
why: Copying increases the count and destroying one owner decreases it, so the object lives while any shared owner remains.
example: Two shared owners address one graph node, and the node is deleted only after both owners are gone.
scenario: Two smart pointers address one node, and the node is deleted only after both pointers have been destroyed. Which type does that?
scenarioWhy: A reference count keeps the object alive until the last sharing owner is destroyed.

definition: A sequence container that stores elements in one contiguous buffer and can grow as elements are added.
wrongs: A linked container whose elements are not required to be contiguous.
A fixed array whose length is set at compile time and cannot grow.
An ordered container of key-value pairs.
why: Contiguous storage provides constant-time indexing, and adding elements may allocate a larger buffer and move the old one.
example: Adding a fourth int when the buffer can hold only three allocates a larger buffer and moves the existing ints.
scenario: A container of ints supports constant-time indexing and may allocate a new buffer when an element is appended. Which container is it?
scenarioWhy: A growable contiguous sequence with random-access indexing is a vector.

definition: An object that designates an element of a container and can be advanced to visit other elements.
wrongs: An integer index, which is the only way to name a position in every container.
A copy of the whole container.
The allocator that obtains memory for the container.
why: Algorithms operate on ranges of these positions, so one algorithm can work with many container types.
example: The begin position of a vector designates the first int, and advancing it once designates the next int.
scenario: A sort is given the first position and the past-the-end position of a vector, not the vector object itself. What are those positions?
scenarioWhy: A range is denoted by iterators that mark elements, including the position just past the last element.

definition: A class that owns a resizable sequence of characters and releases that storage in its destructor.
wrongs: A raw character pointer that stores neither a length nor ownership.
A fixed character array that cannot grow.
A file stream that reads characters from disk.
why: The object tracks its size and buffer, so appending and later destruction are handled by the class.
example: Appending a character may allocate a larger buffer, and destroying the string releases that buffer.
scenario: Code builds text by appending, remembers the length, and frees its buffer when the object is destroyed. Which standard type is that?
scenarioWhy: A resizable owning sequence of characters in the standard library is std::string.

definition: An associative container of unique keys and their values, kept in key order with logarithmic lookup.
wrongs: A hash container of unique keys that does not keep the keys in sorted order.
A sequence indexed only by integers.
A container that allows duplicate keys.
why: Search, insertion, and removal are logarithmic in the number of elements, and walking the container visits keys in sorted order.
example: A map from student id to name stores the smaller id first and finds an id in logarithmic time.
scenario: A container stores one name per student id, walks the ids in sorted order, and finds a key in logarithmic time. Which container fits?
scenarioWhy: Unique keys stored in order with logarithmic operations match std::map.

definition: Giving a class a meaning for an existing operator, such as addition, when an operand has that class type.
wrongs: Changing how tightly an operator binds or how many operands it takes.
Inventing an operator token that C++ does not already have.
Making every operator call a virtual function automatically.
why: The compiler rewrites the operator expression as a call to the function the class provided.
example: A complex type defines addition so that adding two values adds their real parts and their imaginary parts.
scenario: The expression a plus b adds two complex values because the class defined a function for plus. Which feature is that?
scenarioWhy: The class supplied behaviour for an existing operator applied to its type.

definition: A non-member function that a class explicitly allows to use its private and protected members.
wrongs: A member function, which already has access without a friend declaration.
Any function in a derived class, which is a friend of the base automatically.
Any function in the same namespace, which may read private members.
why: Friendship is granted only by an explicit declaration, and it is not inherited by derived classes.
example: A non-member addition for a complex type is declared a friend so it can read the private real and imaginary parts.
scenario: A non-member plus reads the private real part of a complex value, and the class named that function in a friend declaration. Why is the read allowed?
scenarioWrongs: The namespace can read private members
scenarioWhy: The friend declaration grants that non-member access to the private members.

definition: A relationship in which a class contains member objects of other types as parts of its own state.
wrongs: A relationship in which a class derives from another class.
A relationship that uses only a non-owning pointer and stores no member object.
A relationship that makes every function virtual.
why: The member objects are constructed as part of the enclosing object and destroyed with it.
example: A Car type contains an Engine member, so constructing a Car also constructs that Engine.
scenario: Car contains an Engine member that is created and destroyed together with the Car. Which relationship is this?
scenarioWrongs: A non-owning pointer with no member
scenarioWhy: The engine is a part stored inside the car, so the car is composed of an engine.

definition: Declaring several functions with one name and different parameter lists in the same scope.
wrongs: Replacing a virtual function in a derived class while keeping the same parameter list.
Using one function template to generate functions for many types.
Distinguishing two functions only by their return types.
why: Overload resolution selects one of the functions at compile time from the arguments in the call.
example: One print takes an int and another print takes a string, and printing 3 selects the int version.
scenario: Two functions are both named print, one takes int and one takes string, and a call with 3 selects the int version at compile time. What is that?
scenarioWrongs: Choosing a function by return type
scenarioWhy: The same name with different parameter lists in one scope is overloading.

definition: A named scope that groups declarations so they do not collide with the same names in other scopes.
wrongs: A class, which can also hide members with private access.
A function body, which limits the lifetime of its local variables.
A header-guard macro.
why: A name declared in a namespace is found by qualifying it, as with the standard vector name.
example: Two libraries each declare init in their own namespace, and a caller qualifies which init to run.
scenario: Library A and library B both declare init, and the program calls A::init without clashing with B::init. What keeps the names apart?
scenarioWhy: Each init is declared in a different named scope, and qualification selects one of them.

definition: An alias for an existing object that must be initialized and cannot later be reseated to another object.
wrongs: A pointer that may be null and may later be assigned a different address.
A separate copy of an object.
A macro name replaced by source text.
why: Operations on the alias use the object it was bound to, and there is no assignment that makes the alias refer elsewhere.
example: Binding r to x means an assignment to r assigns to x.
scenario: Name r is bound to int x, assigning to r changes x, and r cannot later be made to mean y. What is r?
scenarioWhy: r is another name for x for the rest of r's lifetime, which is a reference.

definition: A constructor that initializes a new object by taking resources from an rvalue and leaving that rvalue valid but empty.
wrongs: A constructor that deeply copies every resource from an lvalue.
An assignment operator that copies into an object which already exists.
A destructor that releases resources without transferring them.
why: The source is expendable, so stealing its buffer avoids copying every element.
example: Returning a local vector can transfer its buffer into the caller's result instead of copying each element.
scenario: A function returns a local vector by value, and the caller can receive that buffer without copying every element. Which constructor performs the transfer?
scenarioWhy: The local vector is an rvalue whose buffer can be taken by the move constructor.

definition: The guideline that if a class defines any special member for a raw resource, it should define or delete all five.
wrongs: A requirement that every class declare exactly five constructors.
Advice to define a destructor for a raw pointer and keep the implicit copy operations.
A limit that a class template may contain only five member functions.
why: A destructor that releases a raw resource usually means the implicit copy would duplicate ownership, so the copy and move operations must be written or suppressed together.
example: A class that deletes a raw pointer in its destructor also defines or deletes the copy and move constructors and assignments.
scenario: A class deletes a raw pointer in its destructor and still uses the compiler-generated copy constructor. Which guideline does that break?
scenarioWrongs: The Rule of Zero, which this class follows
scenarioWhy: Releasing a raw resource in the destructor means the copy and move members must be defined or deleted as well.

definition: The loss of derived members that occurs when a derived object is copied by value into a base object.
wrongs: A virtual call through a base reference that still runs the derived override.
A move of a complete derived object into another object of that derived type.
Deletion of a derived object through a virtual base destructor.
why: The base copy constructor copies only the base subobject, so the extra derived part is not stored.
example: Passing a Dog by value to a parameter of type Animal copies only the Animal part, and the parameter is not a Dog.
scenario: A Dog is passed by value to a parameter of type Animal, and the parameter has none of the Dog members. What happened?
scenarioWrongs: A move of the complete Dog
scenarioWhy: Copying by value into a base object keeps only the base subobject.

definition: A class with more than one direct base class.
wrongs: A chain in which every class has exactly one direct base.
A class that contains several member objects and lists no bases.
Several functions that share one name.
why: The derived object contains one subobject for each direct base.
example: A Phone that derives from both Clock and Radio contains a Clock subobject and a Radio subobject.
scenario: Phone lists both Clock and Radio as direct bases. Which inheritance form is that?
scenarioWhy: Two direct base classes mean the derived class uses multiple inheritance.

definition: The duplicated base that appears when two classes inherit from one class and a fourth class inherits from both.
wrongs: Two functions that cannot be overloaded because their parameter lists match.
A missing virtual destructor in a single base class.
A cycle of shared owners that keeps an object alive.
why: Without virtual inheritance, the most derived object contains two separate copies of the common ancestor.
example: Student and Employee each derive from Person, and a teaching assistant derives from both, so it contains two Person parts.
scenario: A teaching assistant derives from Student and Employee, and each of those derives from Person, making an unqualified Person call ambiguous. What problem is this?
scenarioWhy: Two inheritance paths to Person create two Person subobjects, which is the diamond ambiguity.

definition: A cast that checks at run time whether a pointer or reference in a polymorphic hierarchy refers to the target type.
wrongs: A compile-time cast that performs no run-time check.
A cast that only adds or removes const.
A cast that reinterprets an object's bits as an unrelated type.
why: If a pointer conversion fails, the result is null; if a reference conversion fails, bad_cast is thrown.
example: Converting an Animal pointer to a Dog pointer yields null when the object is actually a Cat.
scenario: An Animal pointer might address a Dog, and failure to convert it to Dog must produce a null pointer. Which cast performs that check?
scenarioWhy: dynamic_cast checks the dynamic type and returns null when a pointer does not address the target type.

definition: Transfer of control from a throw to a matching handler, destroying automatic objects during the unwind.
wrongs: An error code that the caller may ignore, with no destruction of local objects.
Selection of a virtual override.
A directive that stops translation before the program runs.
why: As each scope between the throw and the handler exits, the destructors of its automatic objects run.
example: A function throws a runtime error, the caller's handler prints it, and local objects in between are destroyed.
scenario: A function throws, local objects of the callers are destroyed, and a handler prints the error. Which mechanism did that?
scenarioWhy: throw transfers control to a handler and unwinds the stack, destroying automatic objects.

definition: A standard algorithm that rearranges a random-access range into order and is not required to be stable.
wrongs: A sort that is required to preserve the original order of equal elements.
A container that keeps elements ordered by itself.
The member sort of a linked list, which does not need random-access positions.
why: It needs random-access positions and performs on the order of N log N comparisons.
example: Applying it to a vector containing 3, then 1, then 2 rearranges that vector into 1, then 2, then 3.
scenario: A vector must be fully ordered in about N log N comparisons, and equal elements need not keep their old order. Which algorithm matches?
scenarioWhy: std::sort orders a random-access range and does not promise to keep equal elements in their original order.

definition: A container adapter whose next removal returns the element that was inserted most recently.
wrongs: An adapter whose next removal returns the element that has been waiting the longest.
An associative container from keys to values.
An adapter that always removes the largest element rather than the latest one.
why: The adapter limits a underlying sequence to push, pop, and top so clients use last-in first-out order.
example: After pushing 1 and then 2, top yields 2, and pop removes 2.
scenario: Values are pushed, and the next pop removes the value pushed most recently. Which adapter provides that interface?
scenarioWhy: Removing the most recently pushed element is last-in first-out behaviour of a stack.

definition: In C++, an abstract class that declares only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor, with no data members.
wrongs: A separate interface keyword that introduces a type category C++ does not have.
Any concrete class whose data members are public.
Any header file, whether or not its classes are abstract.
why: C++ expresses a contract as an abstract class of pure virtual operations that derived classes implement.
example: A drawable type contains only a pure virtual draw and a virtual destructor, and Circle implements draw.
scenario: A class has a virtual destructor, only pure virtual functions, and no data, and clients program to that class. What role is it playing?
scenarioWrongs: A type introduced by an interface keyword
scenarioWhy: An abstract class made only of pure virtual operations is the C++ form of an interface.

definition: The operator that copies the state of an existing object into another object that already exists.
wrongs: The constructor that initializes a brand-new object from another object.
The constructor that takes resources from an rvalue to initialize a new object.
The destructor of the source object.
why: The left-hand object is already alive and may already own resources, so assignment replaces that state.
example: After two strings both exist, assigning one to the other copies characters into the existing target.
scenario: String a and string b both already exist, and the statement b = a copies a into b. Which special member runs?
scenarioWhy: b already exists, so the copy is assignment rather than initialization of a new object.
